entries.24778cc7bd8bde5e5176d141218a985e70376273: <div sID="gen12523" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="112" osisID="Ps.112" sID="Ps.112"/> <div eID="gen12523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12524" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12525" type="x-p"/> This psalm is composed alphabetically, as the former is, and is (like the former) entitled "Hallelujah," though it treats of the happiness of the saints, because it redounds to the glory of God, and whatever we have the pleasure of he must have the praise of. It is a comment upon the <reference osisRef="Ps.111.10">last verse</reference> of the foregoing psalm, and fully shows how much it is our wisdom to fear God and do his commandments. We have here, I. The character of the righteous, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. The blessedness of the righteous. 1. There is a blessing entailed upon their posterity, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.2">ver. 2</reference>. 2. There is a blessing conferred upon themselves. (1.) Prosperity outward and inward, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.3">ver. 3</reference>. (2.) Comfort, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.4">ver. 4</reference>. (3.) Wisdom, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.5">ver. 5</reference>. (4.) Stability, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.6-Ps.112.8">ver. 6-8</reference>. (5.) Honour, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.6">ver. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.9">9</reference>. III. The misery of the wicked, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.10">ver. 10</reference>. So that good and evil are set before us, the blessing and the curse. In singing this psalm we must not only teach and admonish ourselves and one another to answer to the characters here given of the happy, but comfort and encourage ourselves and one another with the privileges and comforts here secured to the holy.
entries.890d580d69d0b3a6f19a54da389cf5d77ae0961a: <div eID="gen12525" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12524" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Character of the Righteous.</title> <div sID="gen12526" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> the man <hi type="italic">that</hi> feareth the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">that</hi> delighteth greatly in his commandments. <hi type="super">2</hi> His seed shall be mighty upon earth: the generation of the upright shall be blessed. 3 Wealth and riches <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> in his house: and his righteousness endureth for ever. <hi type="super">4</hi> Unto the upright there ariseth light in the darkness: <hi type="italic">he is</hi> gracious, and full of compassion, and righteous. <hi type="super">5</hi> A good man showeth favour, and lendeth: he will guide his affairs with discretion. <div eID="gen12526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12527" type="x-p"/> The psalmist begins with a call to us to praise God, but immediately applies himself to praise the people of God; for whatever glory is acknowledged to be on them it comes from God, and must return to him; as he is their praise, so they are his. We have reason to praise the Lord that there are a people in the world who fear him and serve him, and that they are a happy people, both which are owing entirely to the grace of God. Now here we have, <div eID="gen12527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12528" type="x-p"/> I. A description of those who are here pronounced blessed, and to whom these promises are made. <div eID="gen12528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12529" type="x-p"/> 1. They are well-principled with pious and devout affections. Those have the privileges of God's subjects, not who cry, <hi type="italic">Lord, Lord,</hi> but who are indeed well affected to his government. (1.) They are such as stand in awe of God and have a constant reverence for his majesty and deference to his will. The happy man is he <hi type="italic">that fears the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.112.1">v. 1</reference>. (2.) They are such as take a pleasure in their duty. He <hi type="italic">that fears the Lord,</hi> as a Father, with the disposition of a child, not of a slave, <hi type="italic">delights greatly in his commandments,</hi> is well pleased with them and with the equity and goodness of them; they are written in his heart; it is his choice to be under them, and he calls them an easy, a pleasant, yoke; it is his delight to be searching into and conversing with God's commandments, by reading, hearing, and meditation, <reference osisRef="Ps.1.2">Ps. i. 2</reference>. He delights not only in God's promises, but in his precepts, and thinks himself happy under God's government as well as in his favour. It is a pleasure to him to be found in the way of his duty, and he is in his element when he is in the service of God. Herein he delights greatly, more than in any of the employments and enjoyments of this world. And what he does in religion is done from principle, because he sees amiableness in religion and advantage by it. <div eID="gen12529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12530" type="x-p"/> 2. They are honest and sincere in their professions and intentions. They are called <hi type="italic">the upright</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.2">v. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.4">4</reference>), who are really as good as they seem to be, and deal faithfully both with God and man. There is no true religion without sincerity; that is gospel-perfection. <div eID="gen12530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12531" type="x-p"/> 3. They are both just and kind in all their dealings: <hi type="italic">He is gracious, full of compassion, and righteous</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.4">v. 4</reference>), dares not do any wrong to any man, but does to every man all the good he can, and that from a principle of compassion and kindness. It was said of God, in the foregoing psalm (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.4">v. 4</reference>), He <hi type="italic">is gracious, and full of compassion;</hi> and here it is said of the good man that he is so; for herein we must be <hi type="italic">followers of God as dear children;</hi> be merciful as he is. He is <hi type="italic">full of compassion, and</hi> yet <hi type="italic">righteous;</hi> what he does good with is what he came honestly by. God hates robbery for burnt-offerings, and so does he. One instance is given of his beneficence (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.5">v. 5</reference>): He <hi type="italic">shows favour and lends.</hi> Sometimes there is as much charity in lending as in giving, as it obliges the borrower both to industry and honesty. He is <hi type="italic">gracious and lends</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.26">Ps. xxxvii. 26</reference>); he does it from a right principle, not as the usurer lends for his own advantage, nor merely out of generosity, but out of pure charity; he does it in a right manner, not grudgingly, but pleasantly, and with a cheerful countenance. <div eID="gen12531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12532" type="x-p"/> II. The blessedness that is here entailed upon those that answer to these characters. Happiness, all happiness, to <hi type="italic">the man that feareth the Lord.</hi> Whatever men think or say of them, God says that they are blessed; and his saying so makes them so. <div eID="gen12532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12533" type="x-p"/> 1. The posterity of good men shall fare the better for his goodness (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">His seed shall be mighty on earth.</hi> Perhaps he himself shall not be so great in the world, nor make such a figure, as his seed after him shall for his sake. Religion has been the raising of many a family, if not so as to advance it high, yet so as to fix it firmly. When good men themselves are happy in heaven their seed perhaps are considerable on earth, and will themselves own that it is by virtue of a blessing descending from them. <hi type="italic">The generation of the upright shall be blessed;</hi> if they tread in their steps, they shall be the more blessed for their relation to them, <hi type="italic">beloved for the Father's sake</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.28">Rom. xi. 28</reference>), for so runs the covenant—<hi type="italic">I will be a God to thee, and to thy seed;</hi> while <hi type="italic">the seed of evil-doers shall never be renowned.</hi> Let the children of godly parents value themselves upon it, and take heed of doing any thing to forfeit the blessing entailed upon the generation of the upright. <div eID="gen12533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12534" type="x-p"/> 2. They shall prosper in the world, and especially their souls shall prosper, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.3">v. 3</reference>. (1.) They shall be blessed with outward prosperity as far as is good for them: <hi type="italic">Wealth and riches shall be in</hi> the upright man's <hi type="italic">house,</hi> not in his heart (for he is none of those in whom the love of money reigns), perhaps not so much in his hand (for he only begins to raise the estate), but in his house; his family shall grow rich when he is gone. But, (2.) That which is much better is that they shall be blessed with spiritual blessings, which are the true riches. His <hi type="italic">wealth shall be in his house,</hi> for he must leave that to others; but <hi type="italic">his righteousness</hi> he himself shall have the comfort of to himself, it <hi type="italic">endures for ever.</hi> Grace is better than gold, for it will outlast it. He shall have wealth and riches, and yet shall keep up his religion, and in a prosperous condition shall <hi type="italic">still hold fast his integrity,</hi> which many, who kept it in the storm, throw off and let go in the sunshine. <hi type="italic">Then</hi> worldly prosperity is a blessing when it does not make men cool in their piety, but they still persevere in that; and when this endures in the family, and goes along with the wealth and riches, and the heirs of the father's estate inherit his virtues too, that is a happy family indeed. However, the good man's <hi type="italic">righteousness endures for ever</hi> in the <hi type="italic">crown of righteousness which fades not away.</hi> <div eID="gen12534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12535" type="x-p"/> 3. They shall have comfort in affliction (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Unto the upright there arises light in the darkness.</hi> It is here implied that good men may be in affliction; the promise does not exempt them from that. They shall have their share in the common calamities of human life; but, <hi type="italic">when they sit in darkness, the Lord shall be a light to them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.7.8">Mic. vii. 8</reference>. They shall be supported and comforted under their troubles; their spirits shall be lightsome when their outward condition is clouded. <hi type="italic">Sat lucis intus—There is light enough within.</hi> During the Egyptian darkness the Israelites had <hi type="italic">light in their dwellings.</hi> They shall be in due time, and perhaps when they least expect it, delivered out of their troubles; when the night is darkest the day dawns; nay, at <hi type="italic">evening-time,</hi> when night was looked for, <hi type="italic">it shall be light.</hi> <div eID="gen12535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12536" type="x-p"/> 4. They shall have wisdom for the management of all their concerns, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.5">v. 5</reference>. He that does good with his estate shall, through the providence of God, increase it, not by miracle, but by his prudence: <hi type="italic">He shall guide his affairs with discretion,</hi> and his God <hi type="italic">instructs him to discretion</hi> and <hi type="italic">teaches him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.28.26">Isa. xxviii. 26</reference>. It is part of the character of a good man that he will use his discretion in managing his affairs, in getting and saving, that he may have to give. It may be understood of the affairs of his charity: He <hi type="italic">shows favour and lends;</hi> but then it is with discretion, that his charity may not be misplaced, that he may give to proper objects what is proper to be given and in due time and proportion. And it is part of the promise to him who thus uses discretion that God will give him more. Those who most use their wisdom see most of their need of it, and <hi type="italic">ask it of God,</hi> who has promised to <hi type="italic">give it liberally,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.1.5">Jam. i. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">He will guide his words with judgment</hi> (so it is in the original); and there is nothing in which we have more occasion for wisdom than in the government of the tongue; blessed is he to whom God gives that wisdom.
entries.6e54e7b6535b864d38fe8e2a389bdbc3607b21e9: <div eID="gen12536" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Blessedness of the Righteous; The Misery of the Wicked.</title> <div sID="gen12537" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Surely he shall not be moved for ever: the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance. <hi type="super">7</hi> He shall not be afraid of evil tidings: his heart is fixed, trusting in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">8</hi> His heart <hi type="italic">is</hi> established, he shall not be afraid, until he see <hi type="italic">his desire</hi> upon his enemies. <hi type="super">9</hi> He hath dispersed, he hath given to the poor; his righteousness endureth for ever; his horn shall be exalted with honour. <hi type="super">10</hi> The wicked shall see <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and be grieved; he shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away: the desire of the wicked shall perish. <div eID="gen12537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12538" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen12538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12539" type="x-p"/> I. The satisfaction of saints, and their stability. It is the happiness of a good man that <hi type="italic">he shall not be moved for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.112.6">v. 6</reference>. Satan and his instruments endeavour to move him, but his foundation is firm and he shall never be moved, at least <hi type="italic">not moved for ever;</hi> if he be shaken for a time, yet he settles again quickly. <div eID="gen12539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12540" type="x-p"/> 1. A good man will have a settled reputation, and that is a great satisfaction. A good man shall have a good name, a name for good things, with God and good people: <hi type="italic">The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.6">v. 6</reference>); in this sense <hi type="italic">his righteousness</hi> (the memorial of it) <hi type="italic">endures for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.112.9">v. 9</reference>. There are those that do all they can to sully his reputation and to load him with reproach; but his integrity shall be cleared up, and the honour of it shall survive him. Some that have been eminently righteous are <hi type="italic">had in a lasting remembrance</hi> on earth; wherever the scripture is read their good deeds are <hi type="italic">told for a memorial</hi> of them. And the memory of many a good man that is dead and gone is still blessed; but in heaven their remembrance shall be truly everlasting, and the honour of their righteousness shall there endure for ever, with the reward of it, in the <hi type="italic">crown of glory that fades not away.</hi> Those that are forgotten on earth, and despised, are remembered there, and honoured, and <hi type="italic">their righteousness found unto praise, and honour, and glory</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.7">1 Pet. i. 7</reference>); then, at furthest, shall the horn of a good man <hi type="italic">be exalted with honour,</hi> as that of the unicorn when he is a conqueror. Wicked men, now in their pride, <hi type="italic">lift up their horns on high,</hi> but they shall all be <hi type="italic">cut off,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.75.5">Ps. lxxv. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.75.10">10</reference>. The godly, in their humility and humiliation, have <hi type="italic">defiled their horn in the dust</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.16.15">Job xvi. 15</reference>); but the day is coming when it <hi type="italic">shall be exalted with honour.</hi> That which shall especially turn to the honour of good men is their liberality and bounty to the poor: <hi type="italic">He has dispersed, he has given to the poor;</hi> he has not suffered his charity to run all in one channel, or directed it to some few objects that he had a particular kindness for, but he has dispersed it, <hi type="italic">given a portion to seven and also to eight,</hi> has <hi type="italic">sown beside all waters,</hi> and by thus scattering he has increased: and this is <hi type="italic">his righteousness,</hi> which <hi type="italic">endures for ever.</hi> Alms are called <hi type="italic">righteousness,</hi> not because they will justify us by making atonement for our evil deeds, but because they are good deeds, which we are bound to perform; so that if we are not charitable we are not just; we <hi type="italic">withhold good from those to whom it is due.</hi> The honour of this endures for ever, for it shall be taken notice of in the great day. <hi type="italic">I was hungry, and you gave me meat.</hi> This is quoted as an inducement and encouragement to charity, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.9">2 Cor. ix. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen12540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12541" type="x-p"/> 2. A good man shall have a settled spirit, and that is a much greater satisfaction than the former; for <hi type="italic">so shall a man have rejoicing in himself alone, and not in another. Surely he shall not be moved,</hi> whatever happens, not moved either from his duty or from his comfort; for <hi type="italic">he shall not be afraid; his heart is established,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.112.7-Ps.112.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. This is a part both of the character and of the comfort of good people. It is their endeavour to keep their minds stayed upon God, and so to keep them calm, and easy, and undisturbed; and God has promised them both cause to do so and grace to do so. Observe, (1.) It is the duty and interest of the people of God not to <hi type="italic">be afraid of evil tidings,</hi> not to be afraid of hearing bad news; and, when they do, not to be put into confusion by it and into an amazing expectation of worse and worse, but whatever happens, whatever threatens, to be able to say, with blessed Paul, <hi type="italic">None of these things move me,</hi> neither will I <hi type="italic">fear, though the earth be removed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.46.2">Ps. xlvi. 2</reference>. (2.) The fixedness of the heart is a sovereign remedy against the disquieting fear of evil tidings. If we keep our thoughts composed, and ourselves masters of them, our wills resigned to the holy will of God, our temper sedate, and our spirits even, under all the unevenness of Providence, we are well fortified against the agitations of the timorous. (3.) Trusting in the Lord is the best and surest way of fixing and establishing the heart. By faith we must cast anchor in the promise, in the word of God, and so return to him and repose in him as our rest. The heart of man cannot fix any where, to its satisfaction, but in the truth of God, and there it finds firm footing. (4.) Those whose hearts are established by faith will patiently wait till they have gained their point: <hi type="italic">He shall not be afraid, till he see his desire upon his enemies,</hi> that is, till he come to heaven, where he shall see Satan, and all his spiritual enemies, trodden under his feet, and, as Israel saw the Egyptians, dead on the sea-shore. <hi type="italic">Till he look upon his oppressors</hi> (so Dr. Hammond), till he behold them securely, and look boldly in their faces, as being now no longer under their power. It will complete the satisfaction of the saints, when they shall look back upon their troubles and pressures, and be able to say with St. Paul, when he had recounted the persecutions he endured (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.11">2 Tim. iii. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">But out of them all the Lord delivered me.</hi> <div eID="gen12541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12542" type="x-p"/> II. The vexation of sinners, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.10">v. 10</reference>. Two things shall fret them:—1. The felicity of the righteous: <hi type="italic">The wicked shall see</hi> the righteous in prosperity and honour and shall <hi type="italic">be grieved.</hi> It will vex them to see their innocency cleared and their low estate regarded, and those whom they hated and despised, and whose ruin they sought and hoped to see, the favourites of Heaven, and advanced to have <hi type="italic">dominion over them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Ps. xlix. 14</reference>); this will make them <hi type="italic">gnash with their teeth and pine away.</hi> This is often fulfilled in this world. The happiness of the saints is the envy of the wicked, and that envy is the <hi type="italic">rottenness of their bones.</hi> But it will most fully be accomplished in the other world, when it shall make damned sinners <hi type="italic">gnash with their teeth,</hi> to see <hi type="italic">Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in him bosom,</hi> to see <hi type="italic">all the prophets in the kingdom of God and themselves thrust out.</hi> 2. Their own disappointment: <hi type="italic">The desire of the wicked shall perish.</hi> Their desire was wholly to the world and the flesh, and they ruled over them; and therefore, when these perish, their joy is gone, and their expectations from them are cut off, to their everlasting confusion; their hope is as a spider's web.  <chapter eID="Ps.112"/> <div eID="gen12542" type="x-p"/>

entries.9e7ecdd310d12f94da8e58f4400eaa857140266e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6818"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 112</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.112.1-Ps.112.10">Psa 112:1-10</reference>. This Psalm may be regarded as an exposition of <reference osisRef="Ps.111.10">Psa 111:10</reference>, presenting the happiness of those who fear and obey God, and contrasting the fate of the ungodly.</title> <div sID="gen10473" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6818"/>1. True fear produces obedience and this happiness. <div eID="gen10473" type="x-p"/>
entries.8b6fb437bca078d121cb11dafd7137c2e6473ae6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6819"/><div sID="gen10474" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6819"/>2-3. Temporal blessings follow the service of God, exceptions occurring only as they are seen by God to be inconsistent with those spiritual blessings which are better. <div eID="gen10474" type="x-p"/>
entries.41fa9c052c98d9ca04cbc556cd434132e70d95db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6820"/><div sID="gen10475" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6820"/><hi type="bold">4. light--</hi>figurative for relief (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.1">Psa 27:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.97.11">97:11</reference>).<div eID="gen10475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10476" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the upright--</hi>are like God (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.36">Lu 6:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.111.4">Psa 111:4</reference>). <div eID="gen10476" type="x-p"/>
entries.01bf57dba04ca0c68d350304e3b14f8f782038c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6821"/><div sID="gen10477" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6821"/>5-9. Generosity, sound judgment in business, and confidence in God, form a character which preserves from fear of evil and ensures success against enemies. While a man thus truly pious is liberal, he increases in substance. <div eID="gen10477" type="x-p"/>
entries.153e3c408caa75fc8760ccb7c929d6d433a3c6a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6824"/><div sID="gen10481" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6824"/>10. Disappointed in their malevolent wishes by the prosperity of the pious, the wicked are punished by the working of their evil passions, and come to naught. <chapter eID="Ps.112"/>

entries.bf5f572f131723e92caa3b87836f36ea41d8d4f2: <div eID="gen22503" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22504" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22505" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22505" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22504" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22506" type="x-p"/> The blessedness of the man that fears the Lord, both as it regards himself and his family, <reference osisRef="Psa.112.1-Psa.112.3">Psa 112:1-3</reference>; his conduct to his family, his neighbors, and the poor, <reference osisRef="Psa.112.4-Psa.112.9">Psa 112:4-9</reference>; the envy of the wicked at his prosperity, <reference osisRef="Psa.112.10">Psa 112:10</reference>. <div eID="gen22506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22507" type="x-p"/> This is another of the acrostic or alphabetical Psalms, under the title Hallelujah. It is formed exactly as the preceding in the division of its verses. It has ten verses in the whole: the first eight contain each two hemistichs, beginning with a consecutive letter of the alphabet; the ninth and tenth verses, three each, making twenty-two in the whole. It is understood to have been written after the captivity, and probably by Zechariah and Haggai: to them it is ascribed by the Vulgate. <div eID="gen22507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22508" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen22508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22509" type="x-p"/> Blessed is the man that feareth the Lord - This seems to be the continuation of the preceding Psalm: there it was asserted that the beginning of wisdom was the fear of the Lord; and here the blessedness of the man who thus fears is stated. <div eID="gen22509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22510" type="x-p"/> That delighteth greatly - It is not enough to fear God, we must also love him: fear will deter us from evil; love will lead us to obedience. And the more a man fears and loves God, the more obedient will he be; till at last he will delight greatly in the commandments of his Maker.
entries.915e23f644b747ed05b8b257283d0eaeed1afa0b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen22510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22511" type="x-p"/> His seed shall be mighty - זרעו zaro, his posterity. So the word should always be understood in this connection.
entries.f40b8ce9fa1af1a6750334041ccb7255c0198ec3: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen22511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22512" type="x-p"/> Wealth and riches shall be in his house - This is often the case: a godly man must save both time and money. Before he was converted he lost much time, and squandered his money. All this he now saves, and therefore wealth and riches must be in his house; and if he do not distribute to the necessities of the poor, they will continue to accumulate till they be his curse; or God will, by his providence, sweep them away. Both צדקה tsedakah and δικαιοσυνη are often used to signify, not only justice and righteousness, but also beneficence and almsgiving; and this is most probably the meaning here. See <reference osisRef="Psa.112.9">Psa 112:9</reference>.
entries.6b5a4179fcbb780cbb674807a101644a3b7fefa0: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen22512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22513" type="x-p"/> There ariseth light in the darkness - The upright are always happy; and when tribulations come, God lifts up the light of his countenance upon him, and causes all occurences to work together for his good. <div eID="gen22513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22514" type="x-p"/> He is gracious, and full of compassion, and righteous - He enjoys the favor of God; that grace makes him compassionate; and in the general tenor of his conduct he is righteous. From these principles he shows favor (<reference osisRef="Psa.112.5">Psa 112:5</reference>) to him that needs it; that is, to the real poor he gives of his substance; and others he obliges by lending, they not being utterly in want, but standing in need only of a little present help. But he takes heed to whom he gives and to whom he lends; that in the first case his bounty may be well applied, and in the second he may not oblige the person who only seeks, under the notion of a loan, to appropriate the money borrowed. To prevent evils of this kind he acts prudently, and guides his affairs with discretion, <reference osisRef="Psa.112.5">Psa 112:5</reference>.
entries.fa2a01ac0499f37f5f03abd02e0c57dda650ad2b: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen22514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22515" type="x-p"/> He shall not be afraid of evil tidings - He knows that God governs the world, therefore he fears not for futurity. And as to the calumnies of men, he fears them not, because his heart is fixed - determined to walk in the path of duty, whatever persecutions he may suffer, for he trusts in the Lord.
entries.25a3993242d750b51694d12e292d81c236e73c7b: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen22515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22516" type="x-p"/> His heart is established - סמוך לבו samuch libbo, "his heart is propped up;" he is buttressed up by the strength of his Maker.
entries.2a95fae0fade940fd5fe3ac3e1caa12151c07862: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen22516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22517" type="x-p"/> He hath dispersed - He has scattered abroad his munificence; he has given particularly to the poor; his righteousness - his almsgiving, his charity, remaineth for ever. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.112.3">Psa 112:3</reference> (note). <div eID="gen22517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22518" type="x-p"/> His horn - His power and authority shall be exalted with honor. He shall rise to influence only through his own worth, and not by extortion or flattery.
entries.50131b8d81f057bd54b72a5fd32348caa689ac96: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen22518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22519" type="x-p"/> The wicked shall see it - רשע rasha, the wicked one. Some think Satan is meant. It is distinguished from רשעים reshaim, wicked men, in the conclusion of the verse. <div eID="gen22519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22520" type="x-p"/> Shall gnash with his teeth - Through spite and ill will. <div eID="gen22520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22521" type="x-p"/> And melt away - Through envy and hopeless expectation of similar good; for his desire in reference to himself and in reference to him who is the object of his envy, shall perish - shall come to nothing.  <chapter eID="Ps.112"/> <div eID="gen22521" type="x-p"/>

entries.1c815d66fb71595818c169b64ba5b24c34fa61b5: <div eID="gen10079" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Alphabetical Song in Praise of Those Who Fear God</title> <div sID="gen10080" type="x-p"/> The alphabetical Hallelujah <reference osisRef="Ps.111.1-Ps.111.10">Psa 111:1-10</reference>, which celebrated the government of God, is now followed by another coinciding with it in structure (<hi type="italic">CTYXOC</hi> <hi type="italic">KB</hi>, i.e., 22 στίχοι, as the Coptic version correctly counts), which celebrates the men whose conduct is ordered after the divine pattern.
entries.07be39b7886f68cef4052fd67d43ab742a355bcb: <reference osisRef="Ps.112.1-Ps.112.10">Psa 112:1-10</reference> <div eID="gen10080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10081" type="x-p"/> As in the preceding Psalm. <reference osisRef="Ps.112.1">Psa 112:1</reference> here also sets forth the theme of that which follows. What is there said in <reference osisRef="Ps.112.3">Psa 112:3</reference> concerning the righteousness of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.3">Psa 112:3</reference> here says of the righteousness of him who fears God: this also standeth fast for ever, it is indeed the copy of the divine, it is the work and gift of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.5">Psa 24:5</reference>), inasmuch as God’s salutary action and behaviour, laid hold of in faith, works a like form of action and behaviour to it in man, which, as <reference osisRef="Ps.112.9">Psa 112:9</reference> says, is, according to its nature, love. The promise in <reference osisRef="Ps.112.4">Psa 112:4</reference> sounds like Isa 60:2. Hengstenberg renders: “There ariseth in the darkness light to the upright who is gracious and compassionate and just.” But this is impossible as a matter of style. The three adjectives (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.111.4">Psa 111:4</reference>, pointing back to <reference osisRef="Exod.34.6">Exo 34:6</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.145.8">Psa 145:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.116.5">Psa 116:5</reference>) are a mention of God according to His attributes. חנּוּן and רחוּם never take the article in Biblical Hebrew, and צדּיק follows their examples here (cf. on the contrary, <reference osisRef="Exod.9.27">Exo 9:27</reference>). God Himself is the light which arises in darkness for those who are sincere in their dealings with Him; He is the Sun of righteousness with wings of rays dispensing “grace” and “tender mercies,” Mal 4:2. The fact that He arises for those who are compassionate as He is compassionate, is evident from Psa 112:5. טוב being, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.10">Isa 3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.17">Jer 44:17</reference>, intended of well-being, prosperity, טּוב אישׁ is here equivalent to אשׁרי אישׁ, which is rendered טוּביהּ דּגברא in Targumic phrase. חונן signifies, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.26">Psa 37:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.21">Psa 37:21</reference>, one who charitably dispenses his gifts around. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.112.5">Psa 112:5</reference></hi> is not an extension of the picture of virtue, but, as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.127.5">Psa 127:5</reference></hi>, a promissory prospect: he will uphold in integrity (בּמשׁפּט, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.2">Psa 72:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">Isa 9:7</reference>, and frequently), or rather (= בּמּשׁפּט) in the cause (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.2">Psa 143:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.23">Pro 24:23</reference>, and frequently), the things which depend upon him, or with which he has to do; for כּלכּל, <hi type="italic">sustinere</hi>, signifies to sustain, i.e., to nourish, to sustain, i.e., endure, and also to support, maintain, i.e., carry through. This is explanatorily confirmed in <reference osisRef="Ps.112.6">Psa 112:6</reference> : he stands, as a general thing, imperturbably fast. And when he dies he becomes the object of everlasting remembrance, his name is still blessed (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.7">Pro 10:7</reference>). Because he has a cheerful conscience, his heart too is not disconcerted by any evil tidings (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.23">Jer 49:23</reference>): it remains נכון, erect, straight and firm, without suffering itself to bend or warp; בּטח בּה, full of confidence (passive, “in the sense of a passive state after a completed action of the person himself,” like זכוּר, <reference osisRef="Ps.103.14">Psa 103:14</reference>); סמוּך, stayed in itself and established. The last two designations are taken from <reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">Isa 26:3</reference>, where it is the church of the last times that is spoken of. <reference osisRef="Ps.91.8">Psa 91:8</reference> gives us information with reference to the meaning of ראה בצריו; עד, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.94.13">Psa 94:13</reference>, of the inevitable goal, on this side of which he remains undismayed. <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.9">2Co 9:9</reference>, where Paul makes use of <reference osisRef="Ps.112.9">Psa 112:9</reference> of the Psalm before us as an encouragement to Christian beneficence, shows how little the assertion “his righteousness standeth for ever” is opposed to the New Testament consciousness. פּזּר of giving away liberally and in manifold ways, as in Pro 11:24. רוּם, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.112.9">Psa 112:9</reference></hi>, stands in opposition to the egoistical הרים in <reference osisRef="Ps.75.5">Psa 75:5</reference> as a vegetative sprouting up (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.17">Psa 132:17</reference>). The evil-doer must see this, and confounded, vex himself over it; he gnashes his teeth with the rage of envy and chagrin, and melts away, i.e., loses consistency, becomes unhinged, dies off (נמס, <hi type="italic">3d praet. Niph</hi>. as in <reference osisRef="Exod.16.21">Exo 16:21</reference>, pausal form of נמס = נמס). How often has he desired the ruin of him whom he must now see in honour! The tables are turned; this and his ungodly desire in general come to nought, inasmuch as the opposite is realized. On יראה, with its self-evident object, cf. Mic 7:10. Concerning the pausal form וכעס, vid., Psa 93:1. Hupfeld wishes to read תּקות after <reference osisRef="Ps.9.19">Psa 9:19</reference>, Pro 10:28. In defence of the traditional reading, Hitzig rightly points to <reference osisRef="Prov.10.24">Pro 10:24</reference> together with Pro 10:28.  <chapter eID="Ps.112"/> <div eID="gen10081" type="x-p"/>

entries.1e1d875da6fd340820653e95b65fb663b04f1aac:
PSALM 112
As the majority of mankind expect to prosper by evil deeds, and as they generally endeavor to enrich themselves by plunder, fraud, and every species of injustice, the prophet enumerates the blessings of God which attend those who worship him in purity, in order that we may know that, in aiming at a life of piety and morality, we shall not lose our reward.
This psalm is also acrostic or alphabetical; and the subject of it being only an enlargement upon the last verse of the preceding, as Muis and others have observed, the same author, it is not improbable, composed both.
Psalm 112:1-3
1. Praise ye Jehovah! Blessed is the man that feareth Jehovah; he will greatly delight in his commandments. 2. His seed shall be powerful in the earth:
“In the earth, or rather, with Green, in the land: as it seems to mean the land of Israel, to which the promise of temporal blessings was limited.” — Dimock.
the generation of the righteous shall be blessed. 3. Wealth and riches shall be in his house: and his righteousness endureth for ever.
 
1 Blessed is the man that feareth Jehovah Although the prophet begins with an exhortation, he has, as I have already pointed out, something farther in view, than simply the calling upon the faithful to praise God. To practice wickedness, and perpetrate injustice, is, in all quarters, accounted a great happiness; and, although integrity may be occasionally praised, nevertheless, there is scarcely one among a hundred who pursues it, because all imagine that they will be miserable unless, by one means or another, they seize as booty every thing which comes in their way. In opposition to this, the prophet tells us that more advantage is to be expected from God’s paternal regard, than from the inflicting of every species of injury, and the perpetrating of every kind of injustice in our power; and by setting before us the certain hope of reward, he calls us back to the practice of equity and beneficence. The following is the analysis which I give of the verse: Blessed is the man that feareth the Lord, and delighteth himself in his commandments; and thus, by the second clause of the verse, the prophet specifies in what the fear of God consists. And that the addition of this explanatory clause is called for, is quite apparent from what we remarked towards the conclusion of the preceding psalm. For, while the law is boldly contemned by mankind, yet nothing is more common than to pretend that they fear God. Such impiety is well refuted by the prophet, when he acknowledges none as belonging to the worshippers of God, but he who endeavors to keep his law. The Hebrew verb חפף, chaphets, is rather emphatical, which is, as it were, to take his pleasure, and I have rendered to delight himself For the prophet makes a distinction between a willing and prompt endeavor to keep the law, and that which consists in mere servile and constrained obedience. We must, therefore, cheerfully embrace the law of God, and that, too, in such a manner, that the love of it, with all its sweetness, may overcome all the allurements of the flesh, otherwise, mere attention to it will be unavailing. Hence a man cannot be regarded as a genuine observer of the law, until he has attained to this — that the delight which he takes in the law of God renders obedience agreeable to him. I now resume the consideration of the passage at large. The prophet, in affirming that the worshippers of God are happy, guards us against the very dangerous deception which the ungodly practice upon themselves, in imagining that they can reap a sort of happiness, I know not what, from doing evil.

entries.10263b228fa64af0a3ec00803b3f69d661f5c5bc:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="112" type="Psalm">
                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>This Psalm containeth a description of a good mans gracious disposition and carriage, as also of his blessed condition even in this life as well as in the next.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Hallelu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jah.</ns0:note> PRaise ye the LORD. Blessed <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the man <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> feareth the LORD <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The fear of God, as it is mans onely wisdom, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 111. 10. so it is his onely way to true happiness.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lighted greatly <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Who makes it his chief delight, care and business to study and obey Gods commandments.</ns0:note> in his commandments <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">He intimates that zeal and fervency in Gods service, is essential to true piety.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 His seed shall be mighty upon earth: the ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neration <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The posterity, as this word is oft used, as <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 23. 43. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 9. 10, &c. called <ns0:hi>his seed</ns0:hi> in the former branch.</ns0:note> of the upright shall be blessed.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Wealth and riches shall be in his house <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Possessed by him whilst he lives, and continued in his family after his death.</ns0:note>: and his righteousness <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The fruit or reward of his righteousness, which is Gods blessing upon his estate: for the work is oft put for the reward of it, as in the Hebrew, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 19. 13. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 7. 2. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 109. 20. And <ns0:hi>righteousness</ns0:hi> may be here taken for his bounty or charity, as it is below <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9. and as this Hebrew word is frequently taken.</ns0:note> endureth for ever.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Unto the upright there ariseth <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 97. 11.</ns0:note> light in the darkness <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">And although he is subject to the troubles and calami<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties of this life, as others are, yet God will give him support and comfort in them, and an happy issue out of them, where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />as the wicked sink under their burdens, and their present mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />series usher in their eternal destruction.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>he</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Either, 1. God. And so this is added as a reason why God causeth light to shine to the upright out of darkness, because the Lord is <ns0:hi>gracious,</ns0:hi> &c. Or rather, 2. the good or upright man, of whom he speaks both in the foregoing and following words. So this is either, 1. a reason why God dealeth thus with good men; it is not from a partial and fond affection to them, but because they are such persons to whom God hath ingaged himself by promise and Covenant to bless them, they are <ns0:hi>gracious,</ns0:hi> &c. Or, 2. as an effect of their affliction and deliverance out of it; thereby they learn to be more <ns0:hi>merciful</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>compassionate</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>just</ns0:hi> or bountiful to others in want and misery.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> gracious, and full of compassion, and righteous.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 A good man sheweth favour and lendeth <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Giveth freely to some, and kindly lendeth to others ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to the variety of their conditions.</ns0:note>; he will guide his <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> words.</ns0:note> affairs <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Maintain and manage his estate or domestick affairs.</ns0:note> with <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment.</ns0:note> discretion <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>with judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment,</ns0:hi> so as is fit and meet, and as God requires, not get<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting his estate unjustly, nor casting it away prodigally or wickedly, nor yet withholding it uncharitably from such as need it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 Surely he shall not be moved for ever <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Though he may for a season be afflicted, yet he shall not be utterly and eternally destroyed, as wicked men shall.</ns0:note>: the righteous shall be in everlasting remem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brance <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Though whilst he lives he may be exposed to the censures and slanders and contradictions of sinners, yet after death his memory will be precious and honourable both with God and with all men, his very enemies not excepted.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 He shall not be afraid of evil tidings <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">At the report of approaching calamities and judgments of God, at which the wicked are so dismayed and affrighted.</ns0:note>: his <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> fixed, trusting in the LORD <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Casting all his care upon God, and securely relying upon his providence and promise.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 His heart <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> established, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Prov. 1. 3</ns0:note> he shall not be afraid, until he see <ns0:hi>his desire</ns0:hi> upon his enemies <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">And although his enemies be many and mighty and ter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rible, yet he shall confidently and cheerfully wait upon God, until he see their ruine and his own deliverance and safety.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Cor. 9. 9</ns0:note> He hath dispersed <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">To wit, his goods, and that freely and liberally, to se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veral persons, as occasion is offered, as this word implies.</ns0:note>, he hath given to the poor; his righteousness <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> His liberality, as this word is used <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 10. 2. & 11. 4. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 4. 27. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9. 9, 10, &c. or the reward of it, as be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3.</ns0:note> endureth for e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Either, 1. his charity is not a transient or occa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sional act, but his constant course, of which he is not weary, but perseveres in it to the end of his life. Or, 2. what he gives is not lost nor cast away, as covetous or ungodly men judge of alms, but indeed is the onely part of his estate, which will abide with him unto all eternity.</ns0:note>; <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Psal. 75. 10</ns0:note> his horn shall be exalted with honour <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Though he may be reproached by ungodly men, yet his innocency shall be cleared, and his name and honour gloriously exalted.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 The wicked shall see <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> and be grieved <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">At the felicity of good men, partly from envy at the happiness of others: partly from his peculiar hatred of all godly men: and partly because it is a plain testimony of Gods justice and providence, and therefore a certain presage of his own ruine.</ns0:note>, he shall gnash with his teeth, and melt away; the desire <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">His desire either of the misery of good men; or of his own constant prosperity and happiness in the world.</ns0:note> of the wicked shall perish.</ns0:p>
               </ns0:div>
